description.narrative: 14,000 girls [aged 0-18 years] and their families in sub-region Dukana Ward. Community leaders, including men and elders, boys, girls and women.

Environmental sustainability: The activities are designed considering natural hazards and adhere to guidelines on DRM and child safeguarding. The availability of the crisis modifier is to allow real-time adaptation and flexibility in project implementation.
Social sustainability: Participants will be equipped with tools and knowledge on how to tackle cultural norms, especially gender bias. In the project several levels of society will be included, such as families, schools, private sector, and government sectors to improve the social environment and social cohesion.

In line with the nexus approach, the first months will focus on urgent (humanitarian) needs. Later phases of implementation will focus on long-term (development) needs, while building community resilience. Throughout, specific activities will focus on child protection while also indirectly contribute towards community cohesion and peacebuilding. In this project we combine humanitarian and development approaches and are working with a Crisis Modifier budget to respond quickly to crisis situations, in order to be more adaptive in our programming in challenging contexts like in Dukana.
Outcome 1: Enhanced community-level resilience and recovery to climate change. ►Activity 1.1: Non-Conditional cash transfers to 238 households. Post-distribution monitoring will be carried out to measure the use and impact of these transfers on nutritional food access, livelihoods and school attendance. ►Activity 1.2: Establish, support and promote VSLA groups for women The project will establish 3 VSLAs, with an expected participation of 20-30 young women in each group. ►Activity 1.3: Conduct community sensitisation and training on dryland farming on climate-smart agriculture Training will focus on dryland farming practices designed to optimise agricultural productivity in water-scarce environments. The training will target 150 farmers in Dukana who will include both men and women. ►Activity 1.4: Provide farming and irrigation tools (and cash for tools), including drip kits, seeds and irrigation equipment. This activity will provide critical farming inputs such as seeds, fertilisers and pest control products that are tailored for dry land agriculture. Irrigation equipment, like drip irrigation systems, will be used to facilitate efficient water use in arid conditions. ►Activity 1.5: Establish and promote 4K Clubs and Young Farmers Clubs in schools These clubs are focused on agriculture and the climate, and will prepare young people for agricultural engagement, climate resilience, market research and careers. In addition to training and exposure related to agriculture, the clubs also provide opportunities for young people to build life skills including leadership, and to participate in events. The activity borrows Plan International’s successful Green Life Skills curriculum. These groups will also be vehicles for transferring information about child rights and as venues for discussion on topics relevant to adolescents and young people such as CEFM, GBV, SRHR, and conflict prevention/resolution. The project will establish 3 clubs, with an expected participation of 40 young people in each group.
Outcome 2: To enhance gender-sensitive access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services ►Activity 2.1: Rehabilitation of community borehole and ongoing maintenance The waterpoint will provide household water, while also contributing to extending water services for small-scale irrigation (see Activities 1.2 and 1.3). Community water committees will be trained in the maintenance of these facilities ensuring that women enjoy meaningful participation and influence in decision making about the borehole and its use. ►Activity 2.2: Capacity building on sanitation and hygiene Capacity building will be done both in schools through the school clubs, school committees as well as through community leaders. Community leaders are the traditionally mandated and influences use of communal resources like seasonal livestock grazing practices, wells and boreholes and therefore they are key decision makers in the operation, maintenance and management of community cultural practice. ►Activity 2.3: Provision of dignity kits 250 kits will be distributed to girls and MHM awareness shall be conducted during the sessions. Boys will also be included as part of raising awareness and breaking the cycle of shame and discrimination. ►Activity 2.4: Supply of handwashing facilities, accompanied by maintenance and cleaning supplies The project will supply handwashing facilities in 3 schools.
Outcome 3: To support women and girls, men and boys to feel safe and empowered to claim their rights ►Activity 3.1: Community sensitisation on child protection, positive gender norms, and conflict mitigation including raising awareness toward existing referral pathways and available services. ►Activity 3.2: Support county-level technical working groups (gender, child protection, health, education, disability). The project will ensure that the voices of Dukana community are heard on issues that continue to affect them. ►Activity 3.3: Support policy forums including dissemination Any local, regional or national policies that are supported by this project (via Activity 3.1 or 3.2) will be disseminated to community members with opportunities for discussion and questions. ►Activity 3.4: Promote meaningful participation of young people. Marsabit County is experiencing an increasing cycle of hazards due to climate change. Over recent years a prolonged drought (ending in late 2023) has resulted in 60-75% loss of livestock. Today, El Niño poses a pending risk of flooding and unpredictable rains (usually during the months of October-December). This all has an implication for the amount and quality of water available for people and their livelihoods (water for livestock and agriculture). The lack of access to clean and reliable water sources increases the risk of disease and malnutrition and affects a sense of dignity.
Women and girls face particular challenges in Marsabit, especially during a crisis. As in many pastoral communities, girls and women are "responsible" for small scale farming and household chores like fetching water - shortages in water and food, insecurity and exacerbated gender norms place women and girls in more labour-intense and dangerous situations, with increased risk for gender-based violence and decreased access to health and hygiene including menstrual hygiene. Girls are at particular risk of FGM/C, CEFM and school dropout.

Plan International Kenya, Plan International Netherlands and Strategies for Northern Development (SND) will form the consortium implementing this project. Plan and SND have a history of collaboration in Marsabit. They worked together in the humanitarian response to the flooding of 2023. With this comes a wealth of experience to build on as well as existing projects and partnerships to leverage. The project will collaborate with relevant government departments and other partners in the thematic area as it contributes to achieving some of results in the county Integrated Development Plan.

SUMMARY. The project addresses the intersectional challenges that girls in Marsabit face especially during a crisis. Marsabit county is home to about 560,000 people who mainly practice pastoralism. The current climate crisis has affected the source of livelihood of the community with a prolonged drought that ended in late 2023 followed by El Nino rains in the last quarter of 2023. The floods have had devastating consequences for girls, women and children, heightening the risk of gender-based violence (GBV), sexual exploitation and abuse. Female headed households and adolescent girls are particularly vulnerable to increased violence, exploitation, and abuse. To address the issues faced by girls in Marsabit, a nexus approach will be applied that must address both their: 1. immediate, lifesaving needs and also their 2. long-term resilience in the face of changing climate and lifestyles, contributing to 3. a more stable and peaceful community.

To address the issues girls face, the response addresses both their 1) immediate, lifesaving needs and also their 2) long-term resilience in the face of changing climate and lifestyles. In combination, these two aspects also contribute to 3) a more stable and peaceful community. Using this “triple nexus” approach, it is expected that girls and their families (and incomes) are better prepared for (climate) crises and are more resilient to the effects of climate change: ✓ Families have better access to nutritious food and drinkable water ✓ Households practice climate resistant farming techniques for better yields ✓ Children and mothers endure less illness and infant mortality ✓ The voices of girls, women, men and boys (including the disabled) are represented in community-level decisions ✓ Girls and their communities have ownership over sustainable solutions that affect them ✓ Men and boys are more aware of the specific needs, strengths and challenges of women and girls ✓ Girls and women feel safer in their communities
Throughout the project, child protection will be prioritised and mainstreamed with a specific lens towards the specific experience and needs of girls.
